questions.question: Explain the difference between primary and secondary socialisation, with examples.

points.text: Primary socialisation: family teaches basic norms (saying please/thank you), language, right/wrong, and core values (honesty, respect). Secondary socialisation: school teaches punctuality, obedience and competition (the hidden curriculum); peers teach group norms and identity; media teaches values and consumer behaviour; religion teaches moral codes.

questions.question: Describe the relationship between norms, values and sanctions.

points.text: Values are broad beliefs (e.g. 'education is important'). Norms are specific rules that put values into practice (e.g. 'attend school every day', 'complete homework'). Sanctions enforce norms: positive sanctions reward conformity (praise for good work), negative sanctions punish deviance (detention for being late). questions.question: Evaluate whether socialisation determines our identity or whether we have free choice.

points.text: Socialisation shapes identity: gender socialisation teaches 'masculine' and 'feminine' behaviour; class socialisation teaches aspirations and tastes; ethnic socialisation teaches cultural traditions. However, individuals also have agency: they can accept, modify or reject socialised norms (e.g. choosing non-traditional gender roles). Neither socialisation alone nor individual choice alone explains human behaviour.
